blocks.text: Masterpiece of the week
London: Interior of the Rotunda at Ranelagh by Canaletto, 1754

blocks.alt: Elegant crowds gather inside Ranelagh’s rotunda beneath an ornate domed ceiling with chandeliers
blocks.caption: Photograph: The National Gallery, London

blocks.text: One of London’s vanished wonders is magically preserved in this masterpiece of perspective painting by an artist better known for his views of Venice. The Rotunda gave 18th-century revellers at Ranelagh Gardens, Chelsea, somewhere to promenade when it was raining or cold outside. Canaletto captures the flirtations, gossip, games and fashionable posing under this spectacular structure in the mid-1750s. It’s a high class, consciously sophisticated urban haunt. There are tables to dine at, privately located in their own arched alcoves, and a full orchestra is playing. The building itself is richly decorated in the rococo style, with a relaxed mix of classical grace and gilded ornament. It looks very European: a grand architectural expression of the rational, science-inspired era known as the Enlightenment. This is not a distorted view of London by Canaletto, but a reminder that the British capital was seen as the Enlightenment’s leading city, its science, coffee shops, commerce and comparatively free speech and satire the envy of continental visitors. The orchestra might be playing Handel, for instance, who worked in London and whose Water Music and Music for the Royal Fireworks reflect the lifestyle we see here. National Gallery, London
